paper_title: Mechanistic Critics for Sample-Efficient NPU Design-Space Exploration

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: NPU design-space exploration for LLM inference mainly relies on an expensive simulator that often returns only scalar feedback such as latency and power. Such feedback can rank evaluated configurations, but gives little information for deciding why a configuration is slow or which architecture parameter should be changed next. This limitation is especially severe because prefill and decode workloads can be limited by different resources, including compute throughput and HBM bandwidth. We propose CriticNPU, a sample-efficient DSE framework built around an online-calibrated mechanistic critic for NPU architecture design. The critic uses explicit hardware limits to evaluate NPU configurations: before simulation, it estimates whether a proposed configuration is likely to improve over the current best and filters weak candidates; after simulation, it aggregates operator-level runtimes into prefill/decode bottleneck summaries and predicts the effect of candidate parameter changes. We instantiate the critic with a Roofline-style model that derives compute and memory limits from architecture parameters and calibrates per-operator-type effective limits using simulator observations. And CriticNPU combines this critic with a workload extractor and an architecture planner to propose configurations. Across six LLM workloads and 16 deployment configurations per model, CriticNPU achieves best-or-tied-best latency in 74% of prefill and 87.5% of decode settings while using roughly half the simulator calls of competitive DSE baselines. We conduct extensive ablation studies and detailed analyses to validate the effectiveness of our method from multiple perspectives. Our code is available at https://github.com/bruno686/CriticNPU.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Neural processing units (NPUs) [Jouppi et al., 2017, Chen et al., 2014, 2016] are specialized accelerators for neural-network workloads and are increasingly important for large language model (LLM) inference [He et al., 2025, Li et al., 2026, Xiang et al., 2026]. Given an LLM specification and deployment setting, NPU design-space exploration (DSE) searches for an NPU configuration that minimizes inference latency under hardware constraints. An NPU configuration is defined by architecture parameters such as systolic-array count and dimension, vector-unit count, clock frequency, on-chip memory size, HBM bandwidth, and interconnect bandwidth, while satisfying power and memory constraints [Chen et al., 2025, Lee et al., 2026]. This search is difficult because architecture parameters interact in coupled and non-smooth ways [Yin et al., 2026]. For example, adding systolic arrays gives little benefit after the workload becomes memory-bound; increasing HBM bandwidth may not help when inter-chip communication dominates; and lowering frequency can sometimes improve latency if it frees power for more parallel units. LLM inference makes the problem harder because prefill and decode often stress different resources, so the best NPU configuration for TTFT may differ from the best configuration for TPOT. 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026). Most DSE methods use simulator to evaluate candidate configurations, but the simulator often returns only scalar feedback such as latencya and power. This feedback can rank evaluated configurations, but it gives little help for deciding which architecture parameter should be changed next. slow configuration may be limited by compute throughput, HBM bandwidth, ICI bandwidth, or mixture of them; scalar latency alone does not reveal which case applies. Black-box search methods, including Bayesian optimization, evolutionary search, and greedy search, can work with scalar feedback [Torun et al., 2018, Bai et al., 2023a, Kao et al., 2020], but they spend simulator calls to learn which regions of the configuration space are useful. Bottleneck-aware methods add more structure by analyzing simulator traces or critical paths [Bai et al., 2023b, Zhang et al., 2026]. They can explain why an evaluated configuration is slow, but the diagnosis is tied to the configuration that was already simulated. It does not directly tell the search procedure whether an unevaluated candidate configuration should be simulated, or which architecture parameters should be prioritized in the next update. Recent LLM-assisted DSE methods can propose multi-parameter configurations from prompts, search history, and design rules [Tang et al., 2025, Wang et al., 2025, Pandit et al., 2025], but deciding whether proposed configuration is worth simulating still needs signal from hardware behavior. This suggests that sample-efficient DSE needs different form of simulator feedback: one that can reject weak candidates before simulation and turn simulated bottlenecks into concrete constraints on the next parameter update. We propose mechanistic critics for sample-efficient NPU design-space exploration. mechanistic critic evaluates candidate configuration through explicit hardware limits, rather than only through scalar simulator score or an LLM-generated estimate. For NPU configurations, these limits correspond to compute throughput, HBM bandwidth, and ICI bandwidth. The critic is used at two points in the search loop. Before simulation, it estimates whether proposed configuration is likely to improve over the current best configuration, so weak candidates can be skipped before calling the simulator. After simulation, it reads the operator-level runtimes, summarizes where prefill and decode latency is spent, and predicts the effect of candidate parameter changes. This diagnosis is then used to constrain the next parameter update. For example, if the simulated configuration is memory-bound, the next update should not simply add more systolic arrays; it should change parameters that affect memory time. Thus, the critic does more than explain evaluated configurations: it also helps choose which configurations to simulate and which parameters to prioritize next. This paper is not about making given edge LLM faster. Instead, it addresses missing first step in edge LLM NPU design: before hardware exploration begins, the system must determine which LLM should become the NPU design target, based jointly on user requirements and hardware constraints. We instantiate the mechanistic critic in CriticNPU, sample-efficient framework for NPU DSE. The critic is implemented as an online-calibrated Roofline-style model [Williams et al., 2009]: for each NPU configuration, it derives compute and memory limits from architecture parameters and calibrates per-operator-type effective limits using simulator observations. CriticNPU has three components. workload extractor (Computing Demand Agent) maps the LLM specification and deployment setting to an operator-level LLM workload. The calibrated mechanistic critic (Online-Calibrated Roofline Model) provides candidate filtering, per-phase bottleneck summaries, and candidate parameter-change predictions. An LLM-based architecture planner (Architecture Design Agent) proposes the next NPU configuration. The planner proposes configurations, while the decision of which candidates to simulate and which architecture parameters to prioritize comes from the calibrated critic. Across six LLM workloads and 16 deployment configurations per model, CriticNPU achieves best-or-tied-best latency in 74% of prefill and 87.5% of decode settings while using roughly half the simulator calls of competitive baselines, including Bayesian optimization, CMA-ES, greedy search, grid search, ChatDSE, LLM-DSE, and LLM-Box. Our contributions are: Framing NPU DSE around mechanistic critics. We formulate sample-efficient NPU designspace exploration as critic-guided search problem, where simulator feedback is used not only to score evaluated configurations, but also to decide which candidate configurations are worth simulating and which architecture parameters should be prioritized next. Calibrating Roofline limits into predictive and diagnostic feedback. We instantiate the critic with Roofline-style model that derives compute, memory limits from NPU architecture parameters and calibrates per-operator-type effective limits using simulator observations. Before simulation, the critic filters weak candidates; after simulation, it summarizes operator-level runtimes into per-phase bottleneck shares and predicts the effect of candidate parameter changes. 2 Reducing simulator cost for LLM inference DSE. We build CriticNPU, sample-efficient NPU DSE framework that combines workload extraction from an LLM specification and deployment setting, critic-guided candidate filtering, and LLM-based configuration proposal. Across six LLM workloads and 16 deployment configurations per model, CriticNPU achieves best-or-tied-best latency in 74% of prefill and 87.5% of decode settings while using roughly half the simulator calls of competitive DSE baselines.

sections.title: 2 Preliminary
sections.content: Problem Formulation. Our goal is to find an NPU configuration with minimal latency for given LLM specification , while satisfying constraints including power, HBM bandwidth and capacity, as well as interconnect and datacenter network bandwidth limits. An NPU configuration θ is joint assignment of architecture parameters (systolic array count and size, clock frequency, HBM bandwidth, ICI bandwidth, etc.) drawn from discrete design space S. Finding the best configuration for LLM inference is constrained optimization, min θS L(θ; W, D) s.t. C, (1) where is the deployment setting (e.g., number of parallel chips). Following standard LLM serving practice, the latency is decomposed into TTFT (time-to-first-token, the prefill phase) and TPOT (time-per-output-token, the decode phase). description of various parameters is in Appendix B. Roofline Model. The roofline model [Williams et al., 2009] provides simple yet effective framework for understanding how efficiently hardware can execute given workload and identifying whether performance is constrained by compute throughput or memory bandwidth. Specifically, it bounds achievable performance as function of arithmetic intensity = FLOPs/Bytes, peak compute throughput C, and memory bandwidth B, expressed as min(C, I). The crossover point Iridge = C/B separates memory-bound operators (I < Iridge) from compute-bound ones (I > Iridge). When deploying LLM on NPU, this classification identifies the primary hardware bottleneck for each operator, providing principled basis for adjusting architecture parameters. For clarity, we provide several illustrative examples in Appendix A.

sections.title: 3 Method
sections.content: CriticNPU treats NPU design-space exploration as mechanistic critic-guided search over NPU configurations. Instead of using simulator feedback only to score evaluated configurations, CriticNPU maintains an online-calibrated mechanistic critic that works at two points in the search loop: before simulation, it filters weak candidate configurations; after simulation, it summarizes prefill/decode bottlenecks and predicts the effect of candidate parameter changes. At the implementation level, CriticNPU has three components, as shown in Figure 1. (1) Compute Demand Agent, implemented as workload extractor, maps the LLM specification and deployment setting to an LLM workload. (2) Online-Calibrated Roofline Model, serving as the calibrated mechanistic critic, derives hardware limits from each NPU configuration, calibrates per-operator-type effective limits from simulator observations, and provides candidate filtering and bottleneck-guided feedback. (3) Architecture Design Agent, an architecture planner, proposes the next NPU configuration using the workload, constraints, search history, bottleneck summaries, and candidate parameter-change predictions. We describe these components in the following sections.

Given the compute, memory limits of candidate configuration, the roofline provides way to estimate whether latency is likely to improve and to identify which operators limit performance. We use this structure to provide performance feedback at two points in the design process. Role 1: Deciding whether candidate is worth simulating. Before invoking the simulator on proposed configuration, we predict its latency from the roofline. sections.title: 4 Experiments
sections.content: To provide fair and thorough evaluation, we test CriticNPU on six LLM specifications ranging from 8B to 671B parameters: Llama3-8B, Llama2-13B, Llama3-70B, Llama3.1-405B, DSv2-236B, and DSv3-671B [Touvron et al., 2023, Liu et al., 2024]. These workloads cover both dense Transformers and mixture-of-experts models. We use NeuSIM [Xue and Huang, 2025], an analytical NPU simulator that reports operator-level latency breakdowns, power, and memory usage for each NPU configuration and workload. We compare against three groups of baselines: black-box optimization methods, including Bayesian optimization (BO) [Torun et al., 2018] and CMA-ES [Sato and Watanabe, 2024]; search heuristics, including greedy local search [Kim et al., 2020] and grid search [LaValle et al., 2004]; and LLM-assisted DSE methods, including ChatDSE [Tang et al., 2025], LLM-DSE [Wang et al., 2025], and LLM-Box [Pandit et al., 2025]. We evaluate all methods across 16 combinations of hardware constraints and deployment settings. Following disaggregated serving, we optimize prefill and decode chips separately: prefill is evaluated by time-to-first-token (TTFT), and decode is evaluated by time-per-output-token (TPOT). TTFT is computed as the latency of processing the input prompt in the prefill stage, while TPOT is computed as the per-token latency of one autoregressive decoding step using the KV cache.

sections.title: 4.2 Detailed Analysis
sections.content: A - Surrogate Accuracy and Screening Reliability. Figure 2 evaluates what gating actually relies on: the ability of the calibrated roofline to rank configurations, and the sim-budget savings it produces when that ranking is used to screen proposals. Panel (a) plots surrogate-predicted against simulated TTFT on 54 proposals from 30-iteration run on Llama3-8B prefill and 50-iteration run on Llama3.1-405B prefill, after normalizing each workload by its median to put both on common scale. The absolute values are noisy, since the theoretical roofline systematically underestimates latency, but the ordering is positively correlated with the simulator within each workload (Kendalls τ = 0.36 on Llama3-8B, 0.41 on Llama3.1-405B), which is what gating requires. Panel (b) shows the practical consequence: over the course of the two runs, roofline-based gating skipped 24 and 46 simulator calls respectively roughly half of every proposal the Design Agent issued. The combined message is that the surrogate does not need to predict absolute latency accurately; it only needs to decide whether candidate is plausibly worse than the current best, and the adaptive-margin gating rule (Eq. 4) uses the moderate but positive ranking signal to prune large fraction of simulator calls without degrading final design quality (cf. Table 1). 8 - Can an LLM Replace the Roofline? Figure 3 asks whether GPT-5.4-mini, the same model CriticNPU uses as the Design Agent, can replace the roofline on the two prediction tasks it performs in the loop. Given identical inputs (workload, reference config with measured TTFT, target config) on 150 Role-1 pairs and 83 Role-2 pairs drawn from the main-table runs, the roofline wins on every metric: 47% vs. 96% MAPE and 5% vs. 21% catastrophic errors on absolute prediction, and τ = 0.62 vs. 0.52 on Role 1 ranking and τ = 0.31 vs. 0.16 on Role 2 TTFT ranking. The LLMs absolute MAPE looks only twice as bad because it hedges by echoing the reference TTFT, since this strategy carries almost no information about which proposed edit is actually an improvement, which is exactly what gating and counterfactual reasoning need. We therefore keep the LLM for high-level design planning and let the roofline do the quantitative surrogate work. - Effect of Online Calibration. Figure 4 shows the effect of online calibration on Llama3-8B prefill: the per-type efficiency factors converge to ηFFN=0.54 and ηattention=0.15, placing the two operator classes under two different effective ceilings rather than one shared theoretical peak. The gap between the two ceilings is not uniform: FFN operators give up about half their peak to cache misses and pipeline stalls, while attention operators forfeit nearly six times more because the softmax dependency serializes work that the matrix-multiply ceiling assumes runs in parallel. The resulting ridge shifts flip the regime label of boundary operators such as layer-normalization and softmax, giving the Design Agent quantitatively correct thresholds rather than single optimistic peak that would mistakenly tag memory-bound ops as compute-bound. This is what lets the gating rule in Eq. 4 prune proposals without losing the good configurations in Table 1, and it is the same calibration signal Role 2 feeds back into the prompt, so the Design Agents next move is grounded in what the hardware actually delivers instead of what it could in principle reach. Figure 4: Calibrated roofline for Llama3-8B prefill. Per-type η pulls the FFN ceiling to 54% and attention to 15% of peak, shifting the effective ridge. - Additional Analyses. Due to page limitations, we defer eight additional analyses to the appendix. Appendix E.1 shows that CriticNPU converges to near-best designs with fewer simulator calls. Appendix E.2 shows stable final TTFT/TPOT across roofline hyperparameters, including gating, EMA, and stopping settings. Appendix E.3 shows that the method generalizes across different agent backbones. Appendix E.4 reports per-deployment results and confirms the aggregate trends across all constraint and deployment settings. Appendix E.5 validates the CDA operator profiles used by the roofline against NeuSIMs native generator. Appendix E.6 shows that CriticNPU reaches near-optimal valid designs faster than baselines under the same simulation budget. Appendix E.7 shows that roofline gating does not discard meaningfully better candidates. Appendix E.8 shows that CriticNPU remains stable under moderate simulator-noise perturbations.

sections.title: 5 Conclusion and Limitations
sections.content: We presented CriticNPU, sample-efficient NPU DSE framework built around an online-calibrated mechanistic critic. The critic turns simulator feedback into practical search guidance: before simulation, it filters weak candidate configurations; after simulation, it summarizes prefill/decode bottlenecks and predicts the effect of candidate parameter changes. Across diverse LLM workloads and deployment settings, CriticNPU reaches near-best latency while using substantially fewer simulator evaluations than competitive baselines. Limitations. Our evaluation is conducted entirely in simulation, without physical implementation or tape-out validation. The results therefore depend on the fidelity of the NPU simulator; online calibration can reduce mismatch within the simulator, but cannot correct systematic simulator errors. The current critic mainly models compute throughput, HBM bandwidth, and inter-chip communication, and may be less accurate for unmodeled effects such as MoE routing imbalance, cross-expert communication, or compiler scheduling artifacts.

sections.title: C Related Work
sections.content: C.1 Architecture-level Design Space Exploration. Architecture-level design space exploration (DSE) directly searches over hardware architectures or microarchitectural configurations, where each candidate corresponds to different processor, GPU, NPU, or accelerator design. For CPU microarchitecture, BOOM-Explorer [Bai et al., 2023a] searches RISC-V BOOM microarchitectural parameters at the RTL level and improves sample efficiency by incorporating microarchitecture domain knowledge into black-box optimization. ArchExplorer [Bai et al., 2023b] introduces bottleneck-aware microarchitecture exploration by constructing microexecution critical paths and reallocating hardware resources according to the identified bottlenecks. ChatDSE [Tang et al., 2025] explores BOOM microarchitectures with GPT-based zero-shot reasoning and pseudo labels to reduce the need for expensive labeled samples. Beyond CPUs, LUMINA [Zhang et al., 2026] performs LLM-guided GPU architecture exploration for LLM workloads by extracting architectural knowledge from simulator code and sensitivity studies. Several works target DNN or AI accelerator architectures. ConfuciuX [Kao et al., 2020] formulates DNN accelerator design as hardware resource assignment and uses reinforcement learning with genetic search to allocate compute and buffer resources under dataflow and platform constraints. AIRCHITECT V2 [Seo et al., 2025] treats accelerator DSE as learning-based recommendation problem, using transformer-based unified representations to recommend accelerator configurations for given workloads and mappings. DiffAxE [Ghosh et al., 2025] casts accelerator design as generative problem and uses diffusion model to generate accelerator configurations conditioned on target performance or energy-delay characteristics. ArchAgent [Gupta et al., 2026] is also related to architecture-level exploration, but focuses on discovering new architectural mechanisms, such as cache replacement policies, rather than only tuning predefined parameters. CriticNPU belongs to this architecture-level category and is most closely related to bottleneck-aware methods such as ArchExplorer and LUMINA. However, unlike CPU critical-path analysis or GPU rule extraction, CriticNPU targets NPU microarchitectural design for LLM inference and uses an online-calibrated roofline model [Williams et al., 2009] to provide 17 operator-level compute, memory, and communication bottleneck signals. This enables candidate filtering before simulation and structured design guidance after simulation. C.2 Implementationand Mapping-level Design Space Exploration. second line of work performs DSE above the architecture level, where the hardware substrate, accelerator template, or compilation flow is largely fixed, and the search focuses on how workload is implemented, compiled, mapped, or deployed. Recently, LLM for engineering [Guo et al., 2024, Kevian et al., 2024, Guo et al., 2025] has become popular. LLM-DSE [Wang et al., 2025] uses multi-agent LLM framework to optimize HLS directive parameters, such as pipelining, tiling, and parallelization choices, for domain-specific accelerators. iDSE [Li et al., 2025] also targets HLS design optimization, using LLM-guided initialization, pruning, and quality-aware refinement to navigate directive configurations. These HLS-level methods can affect the generated circuit quality, but their design variables are directives mediated through synthesis toolchain rather than explicit architecture parameters such as compute arrays, SRAM capacity, bandwidth, or interconnect resources. At the system and mapping level, MLDSE [Qu et al., 2025] provides an infrastructure for exploring multi-level hardware organizations and spatiotemporal mappings across hierarchical accelerators, while LLM-Box [Pandit et al., 2025] guides black-box optimization for mapping LLMs onto specialized accelerator systems through choices such as parallelism, collective communication, KV-cache sharding, and interconnect usage. These works optimize implementation or deployment strategies on given or partially specified substrate. In contrast, CriticNPU directly searches NPU microarchitectural parameters and uses calibrated performance modeling to reason about how changing hardware resources affects operator-level bottlenecks. C.3 Performance Modeling and Bottleneck Analysis complementary line of work develops structured models to capture the relationship between workload characteristics and hardware performance. Analytical models such as the roofline [Williams et al., 2009] provide physics-grounded abstraction of compute and memory limits, while simulatorbased methods perform critical-path or bottleneck analysis to attribute runtime to specific hardware resources [Bai et al., 2023b]. Recent work further leverages LLMs to extract design rules from simulator traces or source code [Zhang et al., 2026]. These approaches expose fine-grained performance structure that is not available from scalar metrics alone, and have been used to interpret simulator outputs or derive design heuristics. However, such models are typically applied after simulation, or used as static predictors that do not adapt to observed execution behavior. Consequently, they provide diagnostic information about existing configurations but are not used to guide exploration before simulator evaluation. Our online-calibrated roofline can also be viewed as physics-informed surrogate specialized to architecture search; unlike statistical surrogate-assisted optimization that requires many initial samples, the roofline becomes useful after as few as 3 calibration rounds due to its strong physics prior. This separation between prediction and optimization limits their effectiveness in reducing the number of simulator calls required for design space exploration.

To separate the two, we score sample efficiency directly: for each (model, deployment, phase) cell we record the lowest valid latency any method reached anywhere in its 100-call trajectorycall this the universal best for that celland then ask each method, how many simulator calls did you need before your best-so-far came within 2% of that universal best? The metric is per-cell scalar (a count, not winner flag), so method that reaches tied-for-best design fast is rewarded equally whether or not another method later finds 0.1% improvement. Configurations that exceed the cells power budget are filtered out before the trajectory is scored. Table 10 aggregates this metric across all six workloads and 16 deployment settings each (96 cells per phase). On prefill, CriticNPU reaches within 2% of universal best in median of 14 simulator calls, 1.6 faster than BO (22), 2.2 faster than Greedy (30), and 3.4 faster than the strongest LLM-only baseline LLM-DSE (47); the mean and 90th-percentile counts confirm the same ordering. The decode-side budget is tighter for everyone because the decode search space is small (CriticNPU: median 8 calls), but the LLM-only baselines that lack physics prior pay clear costLLM-DSE needs 3 more decode calls to reach the same target. The interpretation matches the main-text claim. CriticNPU does not necessarily find strictly lower latency than every alternative on every cellonce budget is unconstrained, several baselines eventually arrive at the same near-optimal designsbut it is the only method that consistently arrives there inside the budget where simulator cost is the binding constraint. ChatDSE never reaches within 2% on any cell because its bypass-the-simulator design routinely exits at power-violating configuration. E.7 Gate False-Reject Analysis The Role-1 gate skips candidate whenever its roofline-predicted latency exceeds the current best (Eq. 4); natural reviewer concern is whether the gate accidentally throws away configurations that would have improved the design if simulated. We test this directly on Llama3-8B decode across all 16 deployment settings: we parse the agent logs to recover every Design-Agent proposal and its decision (simulated or skipped), re-simulate 60 of the 91 skipped candidates with NeuSIM (clean, no noise), and compare the recovered ground-truth TPOT against the best-so-far TPOT at the moment the proposal was issued. We classify skip as false-reject at threshold ϵ iff its actual TPOT undercuts the current best by at least ϵ: Tactual(θskip) < (1 ϵ) . At ϵ=0 (any improvement, however small), 27/60 skipped candidates re-simulate to TPOT below the then-bestbut inspection shows these are essentially ties: in every case the actual TPOT is within 0.01 ms of the best, the consequence of CriticNPUs small decode design space producing many configurations whose runtime collapses onto the same HBM-bandwidth-limited frontier. At ϵ=1% the false-reject rate drops to 0/60; at ϵ=5% it remains 0/60. In other words, the gate never discards configuration that would have meaningfully improved the design. The gating-margin sensitivity in Table 8 is consistent with this: final TTFT/TPOT are unchanged across ϵ0 {0.02, 0.05, 0.10, 0.20}, so the choice of margin only trades simulator calls for nothing on the quality side. E.8 Robustness to Simulator Noise Because the entire evaluation runs inside NeuSIM, separate concern is whether CriticNPU simply optimises simulator quirks rather than discovering generally good NPU configurations. We do not have an alternative simulator or hardware to validate against, so as robustness proxy we inject multiplicative Gaussian noise into NeuSIMs per-operator execution times (and therefore TTFT, TPOT, and chip power) at run time: (o) = (o) (1 + ξo), ξo (0, σ2), σ {0, 0.10, 0.20}. CriticNPU runs inside the noisy simulator (so every gating decision and every Design-Agent reasoning step sees noisy feedback). After each run we re-evaluate the resulting best configuration on the clean simulator (σ=0) to recover its true latency. Table 11 reports the result on Llama3-8B (TP=4, PP=2, BS=16, 300W disaggregated). At σ=0.10 CriticNPU recovers exactly the same end-of-trajectory operating point as the noiseless run (clean-eval TTFT/TPOT identical to four decimal places); at σ=0.20 the search lands on neighbouring configuration with 21% higher true TTFT and 40% higher TPOTdegraded but still well below the typical baseline TTFT on this workload. The simulator-call budget grows by at most 7 calls across noise levels. The gate stays effective because its decision compares predicted latency to the current best, so the multiplicative noise term largely cancels; the EMA-calibrated η(τ ) further damps per-operator noise across iterations. sections.content: 1. Claims Question: Do the main claims made in the abstract and introduction accurately reflect the papers contributions and scope? Answer: [Yes] Justification: The abstract and Introduction state the central contributions: an LLM-driven NPU design framework, an online-calibrated roofline model for pre-simulation screening and post-simulation bottleneck diagnosis, and simulator-efficient NPU design. The claims are supported by the Method section and the experimental results in Section 4, while the paper narrows the scope through the limitations in Section 5. Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that the abstract and introduction do not include the claims made in the paper. The abstract and/or introduction should clearly state the claims made, including the contributions made in the paper and important assumptions and limitations. [No] or [N/A] answer to this question will not be perceived well by the reviewers. The claims made should match theoretical and experimental results, and reflect how much the results can be expected to generalize to other settings. It is fine to include aspirational goals as motivation as long as it is clear that these goals are not attained by the paper. 2. Limitations Question: Does the paper discuss the limitations of the work performed by the authors? Answer: [Yes] Justification: Section 5 includes an explicit limitations paragraph. It states that evaluation is entirely simulation-based, that no physical implementation or tape-out validation is provided, and that results depend on the fidelity of the NeuSIM simulator. Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that the paper has no limitation while the answer [No] means that the paper has limitations, but those are not discussed in the paper. The authors are encouraged to create separate Limitations section in their paper. The paper should point out any strong assumptions and how robust the results are to violations of these assumptions (e.g., independence assumptions, noiseless settings, model well-specification, asymptotic approximations only holding locally). The authors should reflect on how these assumptions might be violated in practice and what the implications would be. The authors should reflect on the scope of the claims made, e.g., if the approach was only tested on few datasets or with few runs. In general, empirical results often depend on implicit assumptions, which should be articulated. The authors should reflect on the factors that influence the performance of the approach. For example, facial recognition algorithm may perform poorly when image resolution is low or images are taken in low lighting. Or speech-to-text system might not be used reliably to provide closed captions for online lectures because it fails to handle technical jargon.
